## 4. Structure theory: completeness, rigidity, robustness

### 4.1 The splitting theorem

**Theorem 4.1 (Splitting).** The map
$$\Phi:\ \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times \times \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times, \qquad \Phi(u,k) = u\,q^{k},$$
is a group isomorphism (writing $\mathbb{Z}$ multiplicatively). Consequently the short exact sequence
$$1 \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times \xrightarrow{\ \operatorname{ord}\ } \mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow 0$$
is split, with splitting $k \mapsto q^k$, and $\operatorname{ord}\circ\Phi(u,k) = k$.

*Proof sketch.* $\Phi$ is a homomorphism because $q^kq^l=q^{k+l}$ and multiplication is commutative. *Injectivity:* if $uq^k=1$ then taking orders gives $k=0$ (as $\operatorname{ord} u = 0$), whence $u=1$. *Surjectivity:* given $x \ne 0$ with $N=\operatorname{ord}(x)$, the shifted series $u := q^{-N}x$ has order $0$, hence is a unit power series, and $x = u\,q^{N}$. The retraction statement is Lemma 2.3. $\square$

**Corollary 4.2 (Kernel description).** $\operatorname{ord}(x) = 0$ if and only if $x$ is an invertible power series. Hence $\ker(\operatorname{ord}) = \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$.

**Theorem 4.3 (Completeness of the invariant).** For nonzero $x,y$:
$$\big(\exists\, u\in\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times:\ x = u\,y\big) \iff \operatorname{ord}(x)=\operatorname{ord}(y).$$
Equivalently $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times/\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times \cong \mathbb{Z}$ via the order, so the order is a *complete* invariant of the coset space: it distinguishes exactly the classes and nothing finer.

*Proof sketch.* ($\Rightarrow$) additivity plus $\operatorname{ord}(u)=0$. ($\Leftarrow$) $xy^{-1}$ has order $0$, so it is a unit power series by Corollary 4.2. $\square$

### 4.2 The cryptographic reading

Define the *pole leak* of a nonzero Laurent series to be $\lambda(x) := \operatorname{ord}(x)$.

**Proposition 4.4 (Blinding invariance).** $\lambda(x u) = \lambda(x)$ for every unit power series $u$; and conversely, if $\lambda(xw)=\lambda(x)$ for some nonzero $w$, then $w$ is a unit power series. Thus the stabilizer of the leak is *exactly* $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$.

**Proposition 4.5 (One-time shift).** $\lambda(x\,q^{k}) = \lambda(x)+k$, and for every target $t\in\mathbb{Z}$ there is a *unique* $k$ with $\lambda(x q^k)=t$, namely $k=t-\lambda(x)$.

Together: the pole order is unmaskable by the $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$-action and perfectly randomizable by the $q^{\mathbb{Z}}$-action — a one-time pad over $\mathbb{Z}$ whose key space is exactly the value group of the valuation.

**Corollary 4.6 (Monster leak).** The class of the moonshine product in $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times/\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times \cong \mathbb{Z}$ is $-194$; it is unchanged by blinding by any unit power series; and $q^{194}$ is the *unique* monomial shift landing the product in $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$.

### 4.3 Rigidity: the order is the only invariant

**Theorem 4.7 (Rigidity).** Let $\varphi : \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times \to \mathbb{Z}$ be *any* group homomorphism (target written additively) with $\varphi(u)=0$ for all $u\in\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$. Then
$$\varphi(x) = \varphi(q)\cdot \operatorname{ord}(x) \quad\text{for all } x \ne 0 .$$
In particular $\varphi$ is an integer multiple of the order, and two such homomorphisms agreeing on $q$ are equal.

*Proof sketch.* By Theorem 4.1 write $x = u\,q^{k}$ with $k = \operatorname{ord}(x)$. Then $\varphi(x) = \varphi(u) + k\varphi(q) = k\varphi(q)$. $\square$

Theorem 4.7 is the precise sense in which the pole-order leak is not one invariant among many: up to a global scalar it is the unique $\mathbb{Z}$-valued multiplicative invariant insensitive to blinding.

**Theorem 4.8 (Why it splits at all).** Every surjective group homomorphism $\varphi : G \twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ from any group admits a homomorphic section. Consequently the splitting in Theorem 4.1 is not an accident of Laurent series but a consequence of the freeness of $\mathbb{Z}$.

*Proof sketch.* Pick $g$ with $\varphi(g)=1$ and let $\sigma(k) := g^{k}$; this is a homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}\to G$ with $\varphi\circ\sigma = \mathrm{id}$. $\square$

**Theorem 4.9 (Uniqueness of the correction, up to blinding).** If $\sigma : \mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times$ is any homomorphic section of $\operatorname{ord}$, then $\sigma(1) = u\,q$ for a *unique* unit power series $u$. Hence $q^{194}$ is the canonical Monster correction up to blinding, and no further ambiguity exists.

*Proof sketch.* $\operatorname{ord}(\sigma(1))=1$, so $\sigma(1)q^{-1}$ has order $0$ and is a unit power series by Corollary 4.2; uniqueness holds because $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$ is a field. $\square$

### 4.4 Torsion-freeness and additive robustness

**Theorem 4.10 (No-Root Theorem).** Let $x \ne 0$ and $n \ge 1$. Then $x^{n}$ is a unit power series if and only if $x$ is. Consequently no positive power of the moonshine product is a power series; indeed
$$\operatorname{ord}\Big(\big(\textstyle\prod_{i=1}^{194} T_{c_i}\big)^{n}\Big) = -194\,n .$$

*Proof sketch.* $\operatorname{ord}(x^n)=n\operatorname{ord}(x)$ by additivity, and $n\cdot k=0$ with $n\ge1$ forces $k=0$ in the torsion-free group $\mathbb{Z}$; then apply Corollary 4.2. $\square$

**Theorem 4.11 (Additive robustness).** Let $f_1,\dots,f_m$ be normalized and let $y$ be any Laurent series (possibly zero) with $\operatorname{ord}(y) > -m$. Then
$$\operatorname{ord}\Big(\prod_{i=1}^m f_i + y\Big) = -m .$$
In particular, adding to the moonshine product any power series, any polynomial in $q$, or any finite sum of series of order $>-194$ leaves the order at exactly $-194$.

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 2.3 the order of a sum equals the smaller of the two orders when they differ; here $\operatorname{ord}(\prod_i f_i) = -m < \operatorname{ord}(y)$. $\square$

Theorems 4.3, 4.7, 4.10 and 4.11 combine into the slogan: the pole-order obstruction is **complete**, **unique**, **indestructible under powers**, and **stable under additive masking**.

## 5. The coefficient hierarchy

Theorem 3.1 records only the leading behaviour. We now compute what lies underneath. Throughout, $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are normalized with coefficient sequences $a_i(0),a_i(1),a_i(2),\dots$, and we set $a_i(-1) := 1$ to encode the leading $q^{-1}$.

### 5.1 The exact convolution identity

**Theorem 5.1 (All-degree formula).** For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
$$\Big[\,q^{\,n-m}\,\Big]\ \prod_{i=1}^{m} f_i \;=\; \sum_{\substack{(\nu_1,\dots,\nu_m)\in\mathbb{N}^m \\ \nu_1+\cdots+\nu_m = n}} \ \prod_{i=1}^{m} a_i(\nu_i-1).$$

*Proof sketch.* Multiply by $q^m$: by Corollary 3.2, $q^m\prod_i f_i = \prod_i P_{f_i}$ is a power series, and the coefficient of $q^{\,n-m}$ in $\prod_i f_i$ equals the coefficient of $q^{n}$ in $\prod_i P_{f_i}$. Expanding the $m$-fold product of power series gives the sum over compositions $\nu$ of $n$ into $m$ non-negative parts of $\prod_i (P_{f_i})_{\nu_i}$, and $(P_{f_i})_{\nu} = a_i(\nu-1)$ with the convention $a_i(-1)=1$. $\square$

Theorem 5.1 is exact but grows combinatorially: the number of terms is $\binom{n+m-1}{m-1}$, already astronomically large for $m=194$ and modest $n$. Its value lies in the collapses it admits.

### 5.2 Low-order collapses without extra hypotheses

**Proposition 5.2 (Leading and subleading).** $\big[q^{-m}\big]\prod_i f_i = 1$ and
$$\big[q^{1-m}\big]\prod_i f_i = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i(0).$$

*Proof sketch.* $n=0$ has the single composition $\nu=0$, contributing $\prod_i a_i(-1)=1$. For $n=1$ each composition places the single unit at one index $i$, contributing $a_i(0)$. $\square$

**Proposition 5.3 (Sub-subleading).** With no hypothesis on the constant terms,
$$2\,\big[q^{2-m}\big]\prod_i f_i \;=\; 2\sum_{i} a_i(1) \;+\; \Big(\sum_i a_i(0)\Big)^{2} \;-\; \sum_i a_i(0)^2 ,$$
i.e. $\big[q^{2-m}\big]\prod_i f_i = \sum_i a_i(1) + e_2\big(a_1(0),\dots,a_m(0)\big)$, where
$$e_2(x_1,\dots,x_m) := \sum_{i<j} x_i x_j = \tfrac12\Big[\big(\textstyle\sum_i x_i\big)^2 - \textstyle\sum_i x_i^2\Big].$$

*Proof sketch.* $n=2$ splits into compositions with a single part equal to $2$ (contributing $a_i(1)$) and those with two parts equal to $1$ at distinct indices $i<j$ (contributing $a_i(0)a_j(0)$). The division-free form avoids dividing by $2$ and is valid over any commutative ring. $\square$

### 5.3 The moonshine collapse

Assume from now on the moonshine normalization $a_i(0)=0$ for all $i$. Then $P_{f_i} = 1 + a_i(1)q^{2} + a_i(2)q^{3} + \cdots$: the *linear* term of each corrected factor vanishes. This single fact pushes the first interaction between two factors from degree $2$ to degree $4$.

**Lemma 5.4 (Quadratic level).** If $g_1,\dots,g_m$ are power series with $(g_i)_0=1$ and $(g_i)_1=0$, then
$$\Big[q^{2}\Big]\prod_i g_i = \sum_i (g_i)_2 .$$

**Theorem 5.5 (Third-order identity).** Under the same hypotheses,
$$\Big[q^{3}\Big]\prod_i g_i = \sum_i (g_i)_3 .$$
Consequently, for $m$ normalized series with vanishing constant terms,
$$\Big[q^{\,3-m}\Big]\prod_{i=1}^m f_i = \sum_{i=1}^m a_i(2).$$

*Proof sketch.* Induct on the number of factors, using the two-factor expansion
$$[q^3](ab) = a_0b_3 + a_1b_2 + a_2b_1 + a_3b_0 .$$
By induction the partial product $\prod_{i<k} g_i$ again has constant term $1$ and vanishing linear term (Proposition 5.2 with $a_i(0)=0$), so the two middle cross terms vanish, leaving $[q^3]\prod_{i<k}g_i + [q^3]g_k$. Transport to the Laurent level via $[q^{3-m}]\prod_i f_i = [q^{3}]\prod_i P_{f_i}$ and $(P_{f_i})_3 = a_i(2)$. $\square$

**Theorem 5.6 (Fourth-order identity).** Let $g_1,\dots,g_m$ be power series with $(g_i)_0=1$ and $(g_i)_1=0$. Then
$$2\,\Big[q^{4}\Big]\prod_i g_i \;=\; 2\sum_i (g_i)_4 \;+\; \Big(\sum_i (g_i)_2\Big)^{2} - \sum_i (g_i)_2^{2},$$
that is, $[q^4]\prod_i g_i = \sum_i (g_i)_4 + e_2\big((g_1)_2,\dots,(g_m)_2\big)$. Consequently, for $m$ normalized series with vanishing constant terms,
$$\Big[q^{\,4-m}\Big]\prod_{i=1}^m f_i \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^m a_i(3) \;+\; e_2\big(a_1(1),\dots,a_m(1)\big).$$

*Proof sketch.* Induct on the number of factors using the two-factor expansion
$$[q^4](ab) = a_0b_4 + a_1b_3 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_1 + a_4b_0 .$$
For the partial product $A = \prod_{i<k}g_i$ we know: $A_0=1$, $A_1=0$, $A_2 = \sum_{i<k}(g_i)_2$ (Lemma 5.4), $A_3 = \sum_{i<k}(g_i)_3$ (Theorem 5.5). With $B = g_k$ satisfying $B_0=1$, $B_1=0$, the expansion reduces to
$$[q^4](AB) = A_4 + B_4 + A_2B_2 ,$$
and $A_2 B_2 = \big(\sum_{i<k}(g_i)_2\big)(g_k)_2$ is exactly the new batch of pairwise products needed to upgrade $e_2$ over $\{i<k\}$ to $e_2$ over all indices, since
$$e_2(x_1,\dots,x_k) = e_2(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1}) + x_k\sum_{i<k}x_i .$$
The division-free formulation follows from the identity $2e_2 = (\sum x)^2 - \sum x^2$; stating the theorem in that form keeps it valid without dividing by $2$. The Laurent statement follows via $(P_{f_i})_2 = a_i(1)$ and $(P_{f_i})_4 = a_i(3)$. $\square$

**Summary table.** For $m$ normalized series with vanishing constant terms:

| degree | coefficient of $\prod_i f_i$ |
|---|---|
| $-m$ | $1$ |
| $1-m$ | $0$ |
| $2-m$ | $\sum_i a_i(1)$ |
| $3-m$ | $\sum_i a_i(2)$ |
| $4-m$ | $\sum_i a_i(3) + e_2\big(a(1)\big)$ |

**Monster specializations.** With $m = 194$ the four rows read: the coefficient at degree $-193$ vanishes; at $-192$ it is $\sum_i c_i(1)$; at $-191$ it is $\sum_i c_i(2)$; and at $-190$ it satisfies
$$2\,\Big[q^{-190}\Big]\prod_{i=1}^{194} T_{c_i} = 2\sum_{i} c_i(3) + \Big(\sum_i c_i(1)\Big)^{2} - \sum_i c_i(1)^2 .$$

### 5.4 Interpretation

The hierarchy has a clean generating-function explanation. Writing $P_i = \exp\!\big(\log P_i\big)$ with $\log P_i = \sum_{k\ge2} \ell_i(k)q^{k}$ (no linear term, because $(P_i)_1=0$), we get
$$\prod_i P_i = \exp\Big(\sum_{k\ge2} L_k q^{k}\Big), \qquad L_k := \sum_i \ell_i(k) .$$
Every coefficient of the corrected product is therefore a universal polynomial in the *power sums* $L_2, L_3, \dots$, with coefficients independent of $m$. Degrees $2$ and $3$ can only use $L_2$ and $L_3$ linearly — there is no way to write $2$ or $3$ as a sum of two or more parts each $\ge 2$ — while degree $4$ admits the partition $4 = 2+2$, which is precisely the source of the quadratic term $\tfrac12 L_2^2$ and, after unwinding, of $e_2$. The first interaction of two distinct factors is thus forced to appear at degree $4$ and nowhere earlier. This is the structural reason for the "three degrees of additivity" phenomenon.

---

## 6. Positivity and domination

McKay–Thompson coefficients for the identity class are dimensions of graded pieces of an infinite-dimensional representation, hence non-negative integers; for other classes they are traces, but non-negativity holds in many cases of interest. The convolution identity converts this into structural statements about the product.

**Definition 6.1.** A complex number $z$ is *non-negative real* if $z = r$ for some real $r \ge 0$. This property is preserved by addition, by multiplication, and by finite sums and products.

**Theorem 6.2 (Positivity propagation).** Let $f_1,\dots,f_m$ be normalized with $a_i(k)$ non-negative real for all $i$ and all $k \ge 0$. Then for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the coefficient $\big[q^{\,n-m}\big]\prod_i f_i$ is non-negative real. Moreover $\big[q^{\,d}\big]\prod_i f_i = 0$ for every $d < -m$, so the statement covers all degrees.

*Proof sketch.* By Theorem 5.1 the coefficient is a finite sum of finite products of the $a_i(\nu_i-1)$ (with $a_i(-1)=1$), and non-negative reals are closed under sums and products. Vanishing below $-m$ is Theorem 3.1. $\square$

**Theorem 6.3 (Coefficient domination).** Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.2, for every index $j$ and every $n \ge 1$,
$$a_j(n-1) \ \le\ \big[q^{\,n-m}\big]\prod_{i=1}^m f_i ,$$
both sides being non-negative reals. In particular the corrected moonshine product grows at least as fast, coefficientwise, as the largest of its McKay–Thompson factors.

*Proof sketch.* In the sum of Theorem 5.1, consider the single composition $\nu$ with $\nu_j = n$ and $\nu_i = 0$ for $i \ne j$; its contribution is $a_j(n-1)\prod_{i\ne j}a_i(-1) = a_j(n-1)$. All other contributions are non-negative reals, so the total is at least this one term. $\square$

Notably the proof is purely combinatorial: an analytic-looking growth estimate falls out of the bookkeeping identity, with no analysis involved.

---

## 7. Numerical instances

We record explicit checks against genuine McKay–Thompson data. Take the three trace series
$$T_{1A} = q^{-1} + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^{2} + 864299970\,q^{3} + \cdots,$$
$$T_{2A} = q^{-1} + 4372\,q + 96256\,q^{2} + 1240002\,q^{3} + \cdots,$$
$$T_{3A} = q^{-1} + 783\,q + 8672\,q^{2} + 65367\,q^{3} + \cdots,$$
all with vanishing constant terms, and form $\Pi := T_{1A}T_{2A}T_{3A}$, which by Theorem 3.1 has order $-3$.

| degree | predicted by | value |
|---|---|---|
| $-3$ | Theorem 3.1 | $1$ |
| $-2$ | Proposition 5.2 | $0$ |
| $-1$ | Proposition 5.3 | $196884+4372+783 = 202039$ |
| $0$ | Theorem 5.5 | $21493760+96256+8672 = 21598688$ |
| $1$ | Theorem 5.6 | $865605339 + 1018360296 = 1883965635$ |

The degree-$1$ entry decomposes as
$$\sum_i a_i(3) = 864299970 + 1240002 + 65367 = 865605339,$$
$$e_2(196884,4372,783) = 196884\cdot4372 + 196884\cdot783 + 4372\cdot783 = 1018360296 .$$
Direct convolution of the truncated series reproduces all five numbers exactly.

Two features are worth noting. First, the jump from $2.2\times10^{7}$ at degree $0$ to $1.9\times10^{9}$ at degree $1$ is dominated by the cross term $e_2$, which exceeds the sum of the individual cubic coefficients: the interaction, once it switches on, immediately dominates. Second, degrees $-2$, $-1$ and $0$ are *exactly additive* in the input data — the three degrees of additivity guaranteed by the vanishing constant terms.

## 8. Algorithms

Three computational procedures follow from the theory.

**(A) Truncated Laurent arithmetic and pole extraction.** Represent a Laurent series by an integer offset $d$ and a coefficient vector $(c_0,\dots,c_{N})$ meaning $\sum_{j} c_j q^{d+j}$. Multiplication is discrete convolution: the product of series with offsets $d_1,d_2$ and lengths $N_1,N_2$ has offset $d_1+d_2$ and coefficients given by the Cauchy product, computable in $O(N_1N_2)$ time (or $O(N\log N)$ by FFT). The order is the index of the first nonzero coefficient, shifted by the offset. Multiplying $m$ series each truncated to $N$ terms costs $O(mN^2)$ by iterated convolution, and the pole order of the result is read off in $O(N)$.

**(B) Symmetric-function coefficient prediction.** Given only the low-order data $a_i(0),a_i(1),a_i(2),a_i(3)$ of $m$ normalized series with $a_i(0)=0$, the coefficients of the product at degrees $-m$ through $4-m$ are computed by the closed forms of Section 5 in $O(m)$ time and $O(1)$ space, using the division-free identity $2e_2 = (\sum x)^2 - \sum x^2$. This is exponentially cheaper than convolution, which would need $\binom{n+m-1}{m-1}$ terms; for $m=194$ and $n=4$ that is over $6\times10^{7}$ compositions versus $194$ additions.

**(C) Blinding, masking and unmasking.** Given a series $x$, a unit power series $u$, an additive mask $y$ with $\operatorname{ord}(y)>\operatorname{ord}(x)$, and a shift $k$, the pipeline $x \mapsto q^{k}(ux) + y$ has order $\operatorname{ord}(x)+k$; recovery of $\operatorname{ord}(x)$ from the transcript is exact and the unique unmasking shift is $k^{\ast} = -\operatorname{ord}(x)$. Each step is $O(N\log N)$ or better, and the leak computation is $O(N)$.

---

## 9. Discussion

### 9.1 What is really being used

Every structural theorem in Sections 3 and 4 is a consequence of two facts: order is additive on products, and its value group $\mathbb{Z}$ is free of rank one and torsion-free. Nothing about $\mathbb{C}$, about modularity, or about the Monster enters. Accordingly, all of Sections 3 and 4 hold verbatim over any field of formal Laurent series over an integral domain, and more generally for any discrete valuation with value group $\mathbb{Z}$ — for instance the $p$-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Q}_p$, where "pole order" becomes "$p$-adic valuation" and "blinding by a unit power series" becomes "multiplication by a $p$-adic unit". The Monster enters only through the numeral $194$ and through the positivity of Section 6.

### 9.2 The cryptographic analogy, and its limits

The analogy with blinding is genuine at the level of group structure: the ambient group is a direct product $K \times \mathbb{Z}$, where $K$ acts as the blinding group and $\mathbb{Z}$ as the leaked value; the leak is a complete invariant of the $K$-orbits, is unique up to scaling among $\mathbb{Z}$-valued invariants trivial on $K$, and is perfectly shifted by the $\mathbb{Z}$-factor. This is exactly the structure one wants of a one-time pad, and exactly the structure one *does not* want of a side channel: any protocol that transmits a formal Laurent series and hopes to conceal its valuation by multiplicative randomization is doomed, no matter how the randomizing unit is chosen.

The limits should be stated as clearly. This is a statement about a specific algebraic invariant of an idealized object, not about a concrete cryptosystem, and the "adversary" here is granted exact algebraic access to the series. What the theory contributes is a complete classification of what such an adversary can and cannot learn from valuation-type queries.

### 9.3 The role of normalization

The coefficient hierarchy shows the normalization $a(0)=0$ doing real work. Without it, interaction begins immediately: the degree-$(2-m)$ coefficient already carries $e_2$ of the constant terms (Proposition 5.3). With it, three degrees are purely additive, and interaction begins at degree $4-m$ with $e_2$ of the *linear* coefficients. Deferring nonlinearity is exactly what makes low-order moonshine identities look like sums of dimensions.

---

## 10. Future directions

**C1. The all-order identity as a complete homogeneous symmetric function.** For a product of $m$ normalized series with vanishing constant terms, we conjecture that the Laurent coefficient at degree $n-m$ is the complete homogeneous symmetric expression in which every partition of $n$ into parts $\ge 2$ contributes exactly once, with multiplicities given by multinomial coefficients over the factors. Equivalently, the generating function of the corrected product is $\exp\big(\sum_i \log(1 + \sum_{k\ge2} a_i(k-1)q^{k})\big)$, so the coefficients are polynomial in the power sums $p_j = \sum_i a_i(j)$ with universal, $m$-independent coefficients. The key insight is that vanishing constant terms make each corrected factor $1 + O(q^2)$, pushing the first interaction from degree $2$ to degree $4$; the degree-$n$ coefficient is therefore a universal polynomial in the power sums with *no* dependence on $m$ until $n=4$, which is exactly what the results at $n=1,2,3$ (pure power sums) and $n=4$ (first cross term, $e_2$ of the linear coefficients) establish. The exact convolution identity over compositions already provides the raw expansion; the remaining work is to organize the collapse by partitions.

**C2. Uniqueness of the leak for non-multiplicative adversaries.** Let $\Phi : \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times \to \mathbb{Z}$ be any function, *not assumed a homomorphism*, that is (i) invariant under multiplication by unit power series and (ii) additive on the subgroup $q^{\mathbb{Z}}$. We conjecture $\Phi = c\cdot\operatorname{ord}$ for some integer $c$. The key insight is that condition (i) forces $\Phi$ to factor through the coset space $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times/\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$, identified with $\mathbb{Z}$ *as a set*, so (ii) upgrades a set-theoretic factorization to an additive one without ever assuming multiplicativity on the whole group. This strictly strengthens the rigidity theorem by removing the homomorphism hypothesis.

**Further avenues.** (i) *Higher orders explicitly*: compute degrees $5-m$ and $6-m$, where the partitions $5=2+3$ and $6=2+2+2=3+3=2+4$ predict mixed symmetric functions, and confirm the multinomial pattern of C1. (ii) *Positivity of cross terms*: since $e_2$ of non-negative reals is non-negative, the domination bound of Theorem 6.3 can presumably be sharpened at degree $4-m$ to $\sum_i a_i(3) + e_2(a(1))$ exactly, giving a two-sided estimate. (iii) *Other valuations*: transport the whole structure theory to a general discrete valuation ring and identify which statements need the residue field to be a field of characteristic zero (none, we expect). (iv) *Replicability*: the McKay–Thompson series satisfy replication formulas; determining how the coefficient hierarchy interacts with replication would connect the elementary bookkeeping here to the deeper moonshine identities.

---

## 11. Conclusion

The order of a formal Laurent series is the simplest nontrivial invariant one can attach to it, and precisely because of its simplicity it is maximally rigid. We have shown that for products of normalized $q$-series of moonshine type the invariant is exactly computable ($-m$ for $m$ factors, so $-194$ for the full Monster product), complete (it classifies series up to multiplication by unit power series), unique (up to scaling, among all $\mathbb{Z}$-valued multiplicative invariants trivial on unit power series), and indestructible (immune to powers and to additive masking of higher order), with a unique repair by the monomial $q^{194}$ — or $q^{193}$ if one wants a normalized series back, the set of normalized series being a torsor under the group of power series with constant term $1$.

Below the leading term, the moonshine normalization produces a striking pattern: three consecutive degrees whose coefficients are pure sums over the factors, followed at degree $4-m$ by the first cross term, the second elementary symmetric function of the linear coefficients. The mechanism — vanishing linear terms in the corrected factors, hence no partition of $2$ or $3$ into parts of size at least $2$ — explains both why the additivity holds and exactly where it must break.

\section{Introduction}

Monstrous Moonshine attaches to each element $g$ of the Monster group $\mathbb{M}$ a
\emph{McKay--Thompson series} $T_g$ depending only on the conjugacy class of $g$. The Monster
has exactly $194$ conjugacy classes, and each series is normalized so that
\[
T_g \;=\; q^{-1} + 0 + a_g(1)\,q + a_g(2)\,q^2 + \cdots,
\]
the identity class giving the normalized modular invariant
\[
T_{1A} = J = q^{-1} + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 + 864299970\,q^3 + \cdots.
\]

The normalization ``leading term exactly $q^{-1}$, vanishing constant term'' is a convention,
but a load-bearing one. A natural structural question is whether the class of such series is
closed under multiplication. It is not: multiplication overshoots, and by an exactly
computable amount. This paper quantifies the failure, shows that it is unremovable in several
precise senses, and computes what lies beneath the leading term.

The rigidity statements have a natural reading in the language of information leakage: the
order of a Laurent series is an integer that no multiplicative blinding, no additive masking
and no exponentiation can perturb, while an explicit and unique monomial shift resets it to
any desired value --- the structure of a perfect one-time pad over $\ZZ$.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
(1) the exact pole order of a product of $m$ normalized series, with the sharp corrections
$q^m$ and $q^{m-1}$; (2) the splitting theorem $\Pow^\times\times\ZZ\cong\Laur^\times$ and the
completeness of the order as an invariant of blinding classes; (3) rigidity,
torsion-freeness, additive robustness and a sharp membership threshold; (4) a torsor theorem
for normalized series; (5) the coefficient hierarchy, exact in all degrees and collapsing to
power sums in degrees $2-m$, $3-m$ and to a second elementary symmetric function in degree
$4-m$; (6) positivity and domination results; (7) explicit numerical instances with genuine
McKay--Thompson data.

\section{Setting and definitions}

\begin{definition}[Laurent series]
A \emph{formal Laurent series} over $\CC$ is a function $f:\ZZ\to\CC$, written
$f=\sum_{n\in\ZZ}f_nq^n$, whose support $\{n : f_n\ne 0\}$ is bounded below. These form a
field $\Laur$ under coefficientwise addition and the convolution product
$(fg)_n=\sum_{j+k=n}f_jg_k$. Series supported in $n\ge 0$ form the subring $\Pow$ of formal
power series.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Order]
For $f\ne0$ set $\ord(f)=\min\{n : f_n\ne0\}\in\ZZ$ and $\ord(0)=+\infty$. The coefficient
$f_{\ord(f)}$ is the \emph{leading coefficient} $\lc(f)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Valuation axioms]\label{lem:val}
For nonzero $f,g$ we have $\ord(fg)=\ord(f)+\ord(g)$, $\lc(fg)=\lc(f)\lc(g)$, and
$\ord(f+g)\ge\min\{\ord f,\ord g\}$ with equality when $\ord f\ne\ord g$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
With $N=\ord f$, $M=\ord g$, the convolution coefficient at $N+M$ has the single nonzero
contribution $f_Ng_M\ne0$, and all lower coefficients vanish termwise. Hence orders add,
leading coefficients multiply and $\Laur$ has no zero divisors. The ultrametric inequality is
immediate, and when the orders differ the lower one is unopposed.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Units and the valuation subring]\label{lem:units}
A power series $u$ is invertible in $\Pow$ iff $u_0\ne0$ iff $\ord(u)=0$; a Laurent series is
invertible in $\Laur$ iff it is nonzero. Moreover $x\in\Pow$ if and only if $\ord(x)\ge0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Normalized series]
A Laurent series $f$ is \emph{normalized} if $f_{-1}=1$ and $f_n=0$ for $n<-1$; we write
$a(k):=f_k$ for $k\ge0$. It satisfies the \emph{moonshine normalization} if in addition
$a(0)=0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Valuation characterization]
$f$ is normalized if and only if $f\ne0$, $\ord(f)=-1$ and $\lc(f)=1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{definition}[Normalized part]
For normalized $f$ put $P_f:=qf = 1 + a(0)q + a(1)q^2+\cdots\in\Pow$, so $(P_f)_0=1$ and
$(P_f)_k=a(k-1)$ for $k\ge1$. Under the moonshine normalization $(P_f)_1=0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Trace series and Monster data]
For $c:\NN\to\CC$ set $T_c:=q^{-1}+\sum_{n\ge0}c(n)q^n$, a normalized series, satisfying the
moonshine normalization iff $c(0)=0$. Every McKay--Thompson series is of this form. Write
$M=194$ for the number of conjugacy classes of the Monster; the product
$\prod_{i=1}^{M}T_{c_i}$ is the \emph{moonshine product}.
\end{definition}

\section{The obstruction and its repair}

\begin{theorem}[Pole-order theorem]\label{thm:pole}
If $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are normalized then $\prod_{i=1}^m f_i\ne0$,
\[
\ord\Big(\prod_{i=1}^m f_i\Big) = -m, \qquad \lc\Big(\prod_{i=1}^m f_i\Big)=1 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on $m$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:val}: each factor contributes order $-1$ and leading
coefficient $1$; orders add and leading coefficients multiply. The empty product has order
$0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Correction to order zero]
$q^m\prod_{i=1}^m f_i=\prod_{i=1}^m P_{f_i}$ has order $0$: it is an invertible power series
with constant term $1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Monster case]
The moonshine product has order exactly $-194$, and $q^{194}$ times it is an invertible power
series with constant term $1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sharp threshold]
For normalized $f_1,\dots,f_m$ and $k\in\NN$, $q^{k}\prod_i f_i\in\Pow$ iff $k\ge m$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The order of the left-hand side is $k-m$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:pole}, and membership in $\Pow$
is equivalent to non-negativity of the order by Lemma~\ref{lem:units}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Renormalization]
If $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are normalized with $m\ge1$, then $q^{m-1}\prod_i f_i$ is again
normalized. In particular $(f,g)\mapsto q\,fg$ preserves the class of normalized series, and
$q^{193}$ times the $194$-fold moonshine product is again of McKay--Thompson shape.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Torsor structure]
Let $\mathcal N$ be the set of normalized series and $G:=1+q\Pow$, a group under
multiplication. Then $G$ acts simply transitively on $\mathcal N$: for all
$f,g\in\mathcal N$ there is a unique $u\in G$ with $f=ug$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$P_f,P_g\in G$ and $u:=P_fP_g^{-1}$ satisfies $ug=f$. Uniqueness holds because $\Laur$ is a
field. Well-definedness of the action follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:val}.
\end{proof}

\section{Structure theory}

\begin{theorem}[Splitting]\label{thm:split}
The map $\Phi:\Pow^\times\times\ZZ\to\Laur^\times$, $\Phi(u,k)=u\,q^{k}$ (with $\ZZ$ written
multiplicatively), is a group isomorphism. Hence
\[
1 \longrightarrow \Pow^\times \longrightarrow \Laur^\times \xrightarrow{\ \ord\ } \ZZ
\longrightarrow 0
\]
is split, with splitting $k\mapsto q^k$, and $\ord(\Phi(u,k))=k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\Phi$ is a homomorphism. If $uq^k=1$ then taking orders gives $k=0$ and hence $u=1$. Given
$x\ne0$ with $N=\ord(x)$, the series $q^{-N}x$ has order $0$, hence is a unit power series,
and $x=(q^{-N}x)q^{N}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Kernel]\label{cor:kernel}
$\ord(x)=0$ if and only if $x$ is an invertible power series; thus $\ker(\ord)=\Pow^\times$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Completeness of the invariant]
For nonzero $x,y$ we have $x=uy$ for some $u\in\Pow^\times$ if and only if
$\ord(x)=\ord(y)$. Equivalently $\Laur^\times/\Pow^\times\cong\ZZ$ via the order.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{The leak reading}

Write $\lambda(x):=\ord(x)$ for the \emph{pole leak} of a nonzero series.

\begin{proposition}[Blinding invariance]
$\lambda(xu)=\lambda(x)$ for every unit power series $u$; conversely, if
$\lambda(xw)=\lambda(x)$ for some nonzero $w$, then $w$ is a unit power series. The
stabilizer of the leak is exactly $\Pow^\times$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[One-time shift]
$\lambda(xq^{k})=\lambda(x)+k$, and for every $t\in\ZZ$ there is a unique $k$ with
$\lambda(xq^{k})=t$, namely $k=t-\lambda(x)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{corollary}[Monster leak]
The class of the moonshine product in $\Laur^\times/\Pow^\times\cong\ZZ$ is $-194$; it is
unchanged by blinding; and $q^{194}$ is the unique monomial shift landing the product in
$\Pow^\times$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Rigidity]\label{thm:rigid}
Let $\varphi:\Laur^\times\to\ZZ$ be any group homomorphism with $\varphi(u)=0$ for all
$u\in\Pow^\times$. Then $\varphi(x)=\varphi(q)\cdot\ord(x)$ for all $x\ne0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $x=uq^{k}$ with $k=\ord(x)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:split}; then
$\varphi(x)=\varphi(u)+k\varphi(q)=k\varphi(q)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Why it splits]
Every surjective homomorphism $\varphi:G\twoheadrightarrow\ZZ$ from any group admits a
homomorphic section: pick $g$ with $\varphi(g)=1$ and set $\sigma(k)=g^{k}$. The splitting of
Theorem~\ref{thm:split} is therefore an instance of the freeness of $\ZZ$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniqueness of the correction up to blinding]
If $\sigma:\ZZ\to\Laur^\times$ is a homomorphic section of $\ord$, then $\sigma(1)=uq$ for a
unique unit power series $u$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[No-root theorem]
Let $x\ne0$ and $n\ge1$. Then $x^{n}$ is a unit power series iff $x$ is. Consequently no
positive power of the moonshine product is a power series; the $n$-th power has order
$-194n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\ord(x^n)=n\ord(x)$, and $nk=0$ with $n\ge1$ forces $k=0$ in the torsion-free group $\ZZ$;
apply Corollary~\ref{cor:kernel}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Additive robustness]
Let $f_1,\dots,f_m$ be normalized and let $y$ satisfy $\ord(y)>-m$. Then
$\ord\big(\prod_i f_i + y\big)=-m$. In particular adding any power series, any polynomial in
$q$, or any finite sum of series of order $>-194$ leaves the moonshine order at $-194$.
\end{theorem}

\section{The coefficient hierarchy}

Throughout, $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are normalized with coefficients $a_i(k)$, and $a_i(-1):=1$
encodes the leading $q^{-1}$.

\begin{theorem}[All-degree convolution]\label{thm:conv}
For every $n\in\NN$,
\[
\big[q^{\,n-m}\big]\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_i
\;=\;\sum_{\substack{(\nu_1,\dots,\nu_m)\in\NN^m\\ \nu_1+\cdots+\nu_m=n}}\;
\prod_{i=1}^{m}a_i(\nu_i-1).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The coefficient of $q^{n-m}$ in $\prod_i f_i$ equals the coefficient of $q^{n}$ in the power
series $q^{m}\prod_i f_i=\prod_i P_{f_i}$; expanding the latter gives the sum over
compositions, and $(P_{f_i})_{\nu}=a_i(\nu-1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Leading and subleading]
$\big[q^{-m}\big]\prod_i f_i=1$ and $\big[q^{1-m}\big]\prod_i f_i=\sum_i a_i(0)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Sub-subleading]\label{prop:second}
With no hypothesis on the constant terms,
\[
2\big[q^{2-m}\big]\prod_i f_i \;=\; 2\sum_i a_i(1) + \Big(\sum_i a_i(0)\Big)^{2}
- \sum_i a_i(0)^{2},
\]
i.e.\ $\big[q^{2-m}\big]\prod_i f_i=\sum_i a_i(1)+e_2\big(a_1(0),\dots,a_m(0)\big)$, where
$e_2(x)=\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j=\tfrac12\big[(\sum_i x_i)^2-\sum_i x_i^2\big]$.
\end{proposition}

From here on assume the moonshine normalization $a_i(0)=0$, so that each corrected factor is
$P_{f_i}=1+a_i(1)q^{2}+a_i(2)q^{3}+\cdots$ with vanishing linear term.

\begin{lemma}[Quadratic level]\label{lem:quad}
If $g_1,\dots,g_m$ are power series with $(g_i)_0=1$ and $(g_i)_1=0$, then
$\big[q^{2}\big]\prod_i g_i=\sum_i (g_i)_2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Third-order identity]\label{thm:third}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:quad}, $\big[q^{3}\big]\prod_i g_i=\sum_i (g_i)_3$.
Consequently, for $m$ normalized series with vanishing constant terms,
\[
\big[q^{\,3-m}\big]\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_i=\sum_{i=1}^{m}a_i(2).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct on the number of factors using $[q^3](ab)=a_0b_3+a_1b_2+a_2b_1+a_3b_0$. The partial
product again has constant term $1$ and vanishing linear term, so both middle cross terms
vanish. Transport to the Laurent level via $(P_{f_i})_3=a_i(2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Fourth-order identity]\label{thm:fourth}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:quad},
\[
2\big[q^{4}\big]\prod_i g_i \;=\; 2\sum_i (g_i)_4 + \Big(\sum_i (g_i)_2\Big)^{2}
- \sum_i (g_i)_2^{2},
\]
that is $[q^4]\prod_i g_i=\sum_i (g_i)_4+e_2\big((g_1)_2,\dots,(g_m)_2\big)$. Consequently,
for $m$ normalized series with vanishing constant terms,
\[
\big[q^{\,4-m}\big]\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_i \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{m}a_i(3)
\;+\; e_2\big(a_1(1),\dots,a_m(1)\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induct using $[q^4](ab)=a_0b_4+a_1b_3+a_2b_2+a_3b_1+a_4b_0$. For the partial product $A$ we
have $A_0=1$, $A_1=0$, $A_2=\sum_{i<k}(g_i)_2$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:quad} and
$A_3=\sum_{i<k}(g_i)_3$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:third}, so with $B=g_k$ the expansion reduces to
$[q^4](AB)=A_4+B_4+A_2B_2$. The term $A_2B_2$ supplies exactly the new pairwise products in
the recursion $e_2(x_1,\dots,x_k)=e_2(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1})+x_k\sum_{i<k}x_i$. The division-free
form uses $2e_2=(\sum x)^2-\sum x^2$ and is valid over any commutative ring.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why three degrees are additive]
Writing $\log P_i=\sum_{k\ge2}\ell_i(k)q^{k}$ (no linear term), we get
$\prod_i P_i=\exp\big(\sum_{k\ge2}L_kq^{k}\big)$ with $L_k=\sum_i\ell_i(k)$. Every coefficient
is therefore a universal polynomial in the power sums $L_2,L_3,\dots$ with coefficients
independent of $m$. Degrees $2$ and $3$ can only use $L_2,L_3$ linearly, since neither $2$
nor $3$ decomposes into two or more parts of size at least $2$; degree $4$ admits $4=2+2$,
which produces the quadratic term and, after unwinding, $e_2$.
\end{remark}

\section{Positivity and domination}

\begin{definition}
A complex number is \emph{non-negative real} if it equals a real number $r\ge0$. This
property is preserved by finite sums and finite products.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Positivity propagation]
Let $f_1,\dots,f_m$ be normalized with all $a_i(k)$ non-negative real. Then
$\big[q^{\,n-m}\big]\prod_i f_i$ is non-negative real for every $n\in\NN$, and
$\big[q^{d}\big]\prod_i f_i=0$ for $d<-m$, so all degrees are covered.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Coefficient domination]
Under the same hypotheses, for every index $j$ and every $n\ge1$,
\[
a_j(n-1)\ \le\ \big[q^{\,n-m}\big]\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_i .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
In Theorem~\ref{thm:conv}, the composition with $\nu_j=n$ and $\nu_i=0$ otherwise contributes
exactly $a_j(n-1)$; all remaining contributions are non-negative reals.
\end{proof}

\section{Numerical instances}

Take the three trace series
\begin{align*}
T_{1A} &= q^{-1}+196884\,q+21493760\,q^{2}+864299970\,q^{3}+\cdots,\\
T_{2A} &= q^{-1}+4372\,q+96256\,q^{2}+1240002\,q^{3}+\cdots,\\
T_{3A} &= q^{-1}+783\,q+8672\,q^{2}+65367\,q^{3}+\cdots,
\end{align*}
all with vanishing constant terms, and set $\Pi=T_{1A}T_{2A}T_{3A}$, of order $-3$.

Here $\sum_i a_i(3)=864299970+1240002+65367=865605339$ and
\[

\]
Direct convolution of the truncated series reproduces all five values exactly. Note that the
cross term at degree $1$ exceeds the sum of the individual cubic coefficients: once the
interaction switches on, it dominates.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{(A) Truncated Laurent arithmetic.}
Represent a series by an integer offset $d$ and a coefficient vector of length $N$ meaning
$\sum_j c_jq^{d+j}$. Multiplication is discrete convolution, costing $O(N_1N_2)$ (or
$O(N\log N)$ by FFT); the order is the index of the first nonzero coefficient shifted by the
offset. Multiplying $m$ series truncated to $N$ terms costs $O(mN^{2})$ by iterated
convolution.

\paragraph{(B) Symmetric-function prediction.}
Given only $a_i(0)=0,a_i(1),a_i(2),a_i(3)$, the coefficients at degrees $-m,\dots,4-m$ follow
from the closed forms in $O(m)$ time and $O(1)$ space via $2e_2=(\sum x)^2-\sum x^2$. For
$m=194$ and $n=4$ this replaces more than $6\times10^{7}$ compositions by $194$ additions.

\paragraph{(C) Blinding, masking and unmasking.}
For a series $x$, a unit power series $u$, a mask $y$ with $\ord(y)>\ord(x)$ and a shift $k$,
the pipeline $x\mapsto q^{k}(ux)+y$ has order $\ord(x)+k$; the unique unmasking shift is
$k^{\ast}=-\ord(x)$.

\section{Discussion}

Every structural theorem above rests on two facts: order is additive on products, and its
value group $\ZZ$ is free of rank one and torsion-free. Nothing about $\CC$, modularity or
the Monster is used, so the structure theory holds verbatim for any discrete valuation with
value group $\ZZ$ --- for instance the $p$-adic valuation, where blinding by a unit power
series becomes multiplication by a $p$-adic unit. The Monster enters only through the numeral
$194$ and through the positivity results.

The analogy with blinding is genuine at the level of group structure: the ambient group is a
direct product $K\times\ZZ$ in which $K$ acts as the blinding group and $\ZZ$ carries the
leaked value; the leak is a complete invariant of the $K$-orbits, is unique up to scaling
among $\ZZ$-valued invariants trivial on $K$, and is perfectly shifted by the $\ZZ$-factor.
Any scheme hoping to conceal a valuation by multiplicative randomization is therefore doomed.
The limits should also be stated: this concerns a specific algebraic invariant of an
idealized object, with the adversary granted exact algebraic access.

Finally, the coefficient hierarchy shows the normalization $a(0)=0$ doing real work. Without
it, interaction begins immediately, the degree-$(2-m)$ coefficient already carrying $e_2$ of
the constant terms; with it, three degrees are purely additive and interaction begins at
degree $4-m$ with $e_2$ of the linear coefficients.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[All-order identity]
For a product of $m$ normalized series with vanishing constant terms, the Laurent coefficient
at degree $n-m$ is the complete homogeneous symmetric expression in which every partition of
$n$ into parts $\ge2$ contributes exactly once, with multiplicities given by multinomial
coefficients over the factors. Equivalently, the corrected product equals
$\exp\big(\sum_i\log(1+\sum_{k\ge2}a_i(k-1)q^{k})\big)$, so its coefficients are polynomial in
the power sums $p_j=\sum_i a_i(j)$ with universal, $m$-independent coefficients.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Non-multiplicative rigidity]
Let $\Phi:\Laur^\times\to\ZZ$ be any function, not assumed a homomorphism, that is (i)
invariant under multiplication by unit power series and (ii) additive on the subgroup
$q^{\ZZ}$. Then $\Phi=c\cdot\ord$ for some $c\in\ZZ$.
\end{conjecture}

Further avenues: compute degrees $5-m$ and $6-m$, where the partitions $5=2+3$ and
$6=2+2+2=3+3=2+4$ predict mixed symmetric functions; sharpen the domination bound at degree
$4-m$ using positivity of $e_2$; transport the structure theory to a general discrete
valuation ring; and study the interaction of the coefficient hierarchy with the replication
formulas satisfied by McKay--Thompson series.

\section{Conclusion}

The order of a formal Laurent series is the simplest nontrivial invariant one can attach to
it, and precisely because of its simplicity it is maximally rigid. For products of normalized
$q$-series of moonshine type it is exactly computable ($-m$ for $m$ factors, hence $-194$ for
the full Monster product), complete, unique up to scaling, indestructible under powers and
additive masking, and repairable in exactly one way. Below the leading term, the moonshine
normalization produces three consecutive degrees of pure additivity followed, at degree
$4-m$, by the first cross term: the second elementary symmetric function of the linear
coefficients.

from __future__ import annotations

import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Number = Fraction

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Truncated Laurent series
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


class Laurent:
    """A truncated formal Laurent series sum_{j} coeffs[j] * q^(offset + j).

    Coefficients beyond the stored window are unknown and treated as truncated away;
    every operation tracks the largest degree that remains exactly known.
    """

    __slots__ = ("offset", "coeffs")

    def __init__(self, offset: int, coeffs: Sequence[Number]) -> None:
        self.offset: int = offset
        self.coeffs: List[Number] = [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs]

    # -- basic accessors -----------------------------------------------------------

    def top_degree(self) -> int:
        """Largest degree whose coefficient is exactly known."""
        return self.offset + len(self.coeffs) - 1

    def coeff(self, degree: int) -> Number:
        """Coefficient of q^degree (zero below the window; error above it)."""
        if degree < self.offset:
            return Fraction(0)
        if degree > self.top_degree():
            raise IndexError(f"degree {degree} is beyond the truncation window")
        return self.coeffs[degree - self.offset]

    def order(self) -> Optional[int]:
        """Smallest degree with a nonzero coefficient, or None if all known ones vanish."""
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c != 0:
                return self.offset + j
        return None

    def leading_coeff(self) -> Number:
        ordv = self.order()
        if ordv is None:
            return Fraction(0)
        return self.coeff(ordv)

    # -- algebra -------------------------------------------------------------------

    def __mul__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        n1, n2 = len(self.coeffs), len(other.coeffs)
        out: List[Number] = [Fraction(0)] * (n1 + n2 - 1)
        for i, a in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if a == 0:
                continue
            for j, b in enumerate(other.coeffs):
                out[i + j] += a * b
        # Only degrees up to min(top1 + offset2, top2 + offset1) are fully determined.
        reliable_top = min(
            self.top_degree() + other.offset, other.top_degree() + self.offset
        )
        new_offset = self.offset + other.offset
        keep = reliable_top - new_offset + 1
        return Laurent(new_offset, out[: max(keep, 0)])

    def __add__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        lo = min(self.offset, other.offset)
        hi = min(self.top_degree(), other.top_degree())
        return Laurent(lo, [self._safe(d) + other._safe(d) for d in range(lo, hi + 1)])

    def _safe(self, degree: int) -> Number:
        if degree < self.offset or degree > self.top_degree():
            return Fraction(0)
        return self.coeffs[degree - self.offset]

    def shift(self, k: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Multiply by q^k."""
        return Laurent(self.offset + k, self.coeffs)

    def power(self, n: int) -> "Laurent":
        result = Laurent(0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (len(self.coeffs) - 1))
        for _ in range(n):
            result = result * self
        return result

    def is_normalized(self) -> bool:
        """True iff the series is q^-1 + a(0) + a(1) q + ... (order -1, leading coeff 1)."""
        return self.order() == -1 and self.leading_coeff() == 1

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        parts: List[str] = []
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c == 0:
                continue
            d = self.offset + j
            parts.append(f"{c}*q^{d}")
        return " + ".join(parts) if parts else "0"


def normalized_series(tail: Sequence[Number]) -> Laurent:
    """Build q^-1 + tail[0] + tail[1] q + tail[2] q^2 + ... ."""
    return Laurent(-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def laurent_prod(factors: Iterable[Laurent]) -> Laurent:
    factors = list(factors)
    if not factors:
        return Laurent(0, [Fraction(1)])
    acc = factors[0]
    for f in factors[1:]:
        acc = acc * f
    return acc


def e2(values: Sequence[Number]) -> Number:
    """Second elementary symmetric function, division-free: ((sum x)^2 - sum x^2) / 2."""
    s = sum(values, Fraction(0))
    sq = sum((v * v for v in values), Fraction(0))
    return (s * s - sq) / 2

MCKAY_THOMPSON: Dict[str, List[int]] = {

def demo_pole_order() -> None:
    banner("1. Pole-order theorem: a product of m normalized series has order exactly -m")
    rng = random.Random(20260819)
    for m in (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13):
        factors = [
            normalized_series([Fraction(rng.randint(-9, 9)) for _ in range(9)])
            for _ in range(m)
        ]
        prod = laurent_prod(factors)
        assert prod.order() == -m, (m, prod.order())
        assert prod.leading_coeff() == 1
        corrected = prod.shift(m)
        renormalized = prod.shift(m - 1)
        assert corrected.order() == 0 and corrected.leading_coeff() == 1
        assert renormalized.is_normalized()
        print(
            f"  m = {m:2d}:  order(prod) = {prod.order():3d},  "
            f"leading coeff = {prod.leading_coeff()},  "
            f"order(q^m * prod) = {corrected.order()},  "
            f"q^(m-1)*prod normalized = {renormalized.is_normalized()}"
        )
    print("  Sharp threshold: q^k * prod is a power series iff k >= m.")
    m = 5
    factors = [
        normalized_series([Fraction(rng.randint(-9, 9)) for _ in range(9)])
        for _ in range(m)
    ]
    prod = laurent_prod(factors)
    for k in range(m + 3):
        is_ps = prod.shift(k).order() is not None and prod.shift(k).order() >= 0
        assert is_ps == (k >= m)
    print(f"    verified for m = {m} and k = 0..{m + 2}.")

def demo_indestructible_leak() -> None:
    banner("2. The leak is indestructible: blinding, masking, powers, unmasking")
    rng = random.Random(11235)
    m = 4
    factors = [
        normalized_series([Fraction(rng.randint(-6, 6)) for _ in range(10)])
        for _ in range(m)
    ]
    prod = laurent_prod(factors)
    print(f"  order of the plain product          : {prod.order()}")

    # Multiplicative blinding by an invertible power series (nonzero constant term).
    blind = Laurent(0, [Fraction(7)] + [Fraction(rng.randint(-5, 5)) for _ in range(9)])
    blinded = prod * blind
    print(f"  order after blinding by a unit series: {blinded.order()}")
    assert blinded.order() == prod.order()

    # Additive masking by any strictly less singular series.
    mask = Laurent(-m + 1, [Fraction(rng.randint(-40, 40)) for _ in range(8)])
    masked = prod + mask
    print(f"  order after additive masking         : {masked.order()}")
    assert masked.order() == prod.order()

    # Torsion-freeness: the n-th power has order -mn.
    for n in (1, 2, 3):
        p = prod.power(n)
        print(f"  order of the {n}-th power              : {p.order()}  (expected {-m * n})")
        assert p.order() == -m * n

    # Unique unmasking shift.
    target = 0
    k_star = target - prod.order()
    assert prod.shift(k_star).order() == target
    others = [k for k in range(-6, 7) if prod.shift(k).order() == target]
    print(f"  unique shift with order {target}: k = {k_star}; all solutions found: {others}")
    assert others == [k_star]

def predicted_coefficients(tails: Sequence[Sequence[Number]]) -> Dict[int, Number]:
    """Closed-form predictions at degrees -m, 1-m, 2-m, 3-m, 4-m (moonshine normalization).

    tails[i] = [a_i(0), a_i(1), a_i(2), a_i(3), ...] with a_i(0) = 0.
    """
    m = len(tails)
    a1 = [Fraction(t[1]) for t in tails]
    a2 = [Fraction(t[2]) for t in tails]
    a3 = [Fraction(t[3]) for t in tails]
    return {
        -m: Fraction(1),
        1 - m: Fraction(0),
        2 - m: sum(a1, Fraction(0)),
        3 - m: sum(a2, Fraction(0)),
        4 - m: sum(a3, Fraction(0)) + e2(a1),
    }


def demo_coefficient_hierarchy() -> None:
    banner("3. Coefficient hierarchy: three additive degrees, then the first cross term")
    rng = random.Random(31415)
    for m in (2, 3, 6, 10):
        tails = [
            [Fraction(0)] + [Fraction(rng.randint(0, 30)) for _ in range(7)]
            for _ in range(m)
        ]
        factors = [normalized_series(t) for t in tails]
        prod = laurent_prod(factors)
        pred = predicted_coefficients(tails)
        print(f"  m = {m}:")
        for d in sorted(pred):
            actual = prod.coeff(d)
            flag = "OK" if actual == pred[d] else "MISMATCH"
            print(f"    degree {d:4d}:  direct = {str(actual):>14}   predicted = "
                  f"{str(pred[d]):>14}   [{flag}]")
            assert actual == pred[d]
        cross = e2([Fraction(t[1]) for t in tails])
        print(f"    of which the cross term e2(a(1)) at degree {4 - m} contributes {cross}")

Number = Fraction

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Truncated Laurent series
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


class Laurent:
    """A truncated formal Laurent series sum_{j} coeffs[j] * q^(offset + j).

    Coefficients beyond the stored window are unknown and treated as truncated away;
    every operation tracks the largest degree that remains exactly known.
    """

    __slots__ = ("offset", "coeffs")

    def __init__(self, offset: int, coeffs: Sequence[Number]) -> None:
        self.offset: int = offset
        self.coeffs: List[Number] = [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs]

    # -- basic accessors -----------------------------------------------------------

    def top_degree(self) -> int:
        """Largest degree whose coefficient is exactly known."""
        return self.offset + len(self.coeffs) - 1

    def coeff(self, degree: int) -> Number:
        """Coefficient of q^degree (zero below the window; error above it)."""
        if degree < self.offset:
            return Fraction(0)
        if degree > self.top_degree():
            raise IndexError(f"degree {degree} is beyond the truncation window")
        return self.coeffs[degree - self.offset]

    def order(self) -> Optional[int]:
        """Smallest degree with a nonzero coefficient, or None if all known ones vanish."""
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c != 0:
                return self.offset + j
        return None

    def leading_coeff(self) -> Number:
        ordv = self.order()
        if ordv is None:
            return Fraction(0)
        return self.coeff(ordv)

    # -- algebra -------------------------------------------------------------------

    def __mul__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        n1, n2 = len(self.coeffs), len(other.coeffs)
        out: List[Number] = [Fraction(0)] * (n1 + n2 - 1)
        for i, a in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if a == 0:
                continue
            for j, b in enumerate(other.coeffs):
                out[i + j] += a * b
        # Only degrees up to min(top1 + offset2, top2 + offset1) are fully determined.
        reliable_top = min(
            self.top_degree() + other.offset, other.top_degree() + self.offset
        )
        new_offset = self.offset + other.offset
        keep = reliable_top - new_offset + 1
        return Laurent(new_offset, out[: max(keep, 0)])

    def __add__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        lo = min(self.offset, other.offset)
        hi = min(self.top_degree(), other.top_degree())
        return Laurent(lo, [self._safe(d) + other._safe(d) for d in range(lo, hi + 1)])

    def _safe(self, degree: int) -> Number:
        if degree < self.offset or degree > self.top_degree():
            return Fraction(0)
        return self.coeffs[degree - self.offset]

    def shift(self, k: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Multiply by q^k."""
        return Laurent(self.offset + k, self.coeffs)

    def power(self, n: int) -> "Laurent":
        result = Laurent(0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (len(self.coeffs) - 1))
        for _ in range(n):
            result = result * self
        return result

    def is_normalized(self) -> bool:
        """True iff the series is q^-1 + a(0) + a(1) q + ... (order -1, leading coeff 1)."""
        return self.order() == -1 and self.leading_coeff() == 1

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        parts: List[str] = []
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c == 0:
                continue
            d = self.offset + j
            parts.append(f"{c}*q^{d}")
        return " + ".join(parts) if parts else "0"


def normalized_series(tail: Sequence[Number]) -> Laurent:
    """Build q^-1 + tail[0] + tail[1] q + tail[2] q^2 + ... ."""
    return Laurent(-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def laurent_prod(factors: Iterable[Laurent]) -> Laurent:
    factors = list(factors)
    if not factors:
        return Laurent(0, [Fraction(1)])
    acc = factors[0]
    for f in factors[1:]:
        acc = acc * f
    return acc


def e2(values: Sequence[Number]) -> Number:
    """Second elementary symmetric function, division-free: ((sum x)^2 - sum x^2) / 2."""
    s = sum(values, Fraction(0))
    sq = sum((v * v for v in values), Fraction(0))
    return (s * s - sq) / 2

def predicted_coefficients(tails: Sequence[Sequence[Number]]) -> Dict[int, Number]:
    """Closed-form predictions at degrees -m, 1-m, 2-m, 3-m, 4-m (moonshine normalization).

    tails[i] = [a_i(0), a_i(1), a_i(2), a_i(3), ...] with a_i(0) = 0.

    a1 = [Fraction(t[1]) for t in tails]

        -m: Fraction(1),
        1 - m: Fraction(0),
        2 - m: sum(a1, Fraction(0)),
        3 - m: sum(a2, Fraction(0)),
        4 - m: sum(a3, Fraction(0)) + e2(a1),
    }

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

Series = Tuple[int, List[Fraction]]


def normalized(tail: Sequence[object]) -> Series:
    return -1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail]  # type: ignore[arg-type]


def top(x: Series) -> int:
    return x[0] + len(x[1]) - 1


def mul(x: Series, y: Series) -> Series:
    dx, cx = x
    dy, cy = y
    raw = [Fraction(0)] * (len(cx) + len(cy) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(cx):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cy):
            raw[i + j] += a * b
    off = dx + dy
    keep = min(top(x) + dy, top(y) + dx) - off + 1
    return off, raw[: max(keep, 0)]


def prod(fs: Sequence[Series]) -> Series:
    acc = fs[0]
    for f in fs[1:]:
        acc = mul(acc, f)
    return acc

    if n == 0:
        return Fraction(1)
    return sum((Fraction(t[n - 1]) for t in tails), Fraction(0))

    m = len(tails)
    p = prod([normalized(t) for t in tails])
    for n in range(0, depth + 1):
        d = n - m
        if d > top(p):
            return None
        if coeff(p, d) != additive_prediction(tails, n):
            return d
    return None

    m = len(tails)
    p = prod([normalized(t) for t in tails])
    print(f"\n  {label}   (m = {m})")
    print("    degree | true coefficient | additive guess | interaction")
    for n in range(0, 5):
        d = n - m
        if d > top(p):
            break
        true_c = coeff(p, d)
        guess = additive_prediction(tails, n)
        gap = true_c - guess
        marker = "" if gap == 0 else f"  <-- cross term {gap}"
        print(f"    {d:6d} | {str(true_c):>16} | {str(guess):>14} |{marker}")
    fid = first_interaction_degree(tails, 4)
    print(f"    first interaction at degree {fid}  (i.e. n = {fid + m if fid is not None else '-'})")

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple

LaurentSeries = Tuple[int, List[Fraction]]  # (offset d, coefficients of q^d, q^(d+1), ...)


def make_series(offset: int, coeffs: Sequence[object]) -> LaurentSeries:
    """Build a truncated Laurent series sum_j coeffs[j] q^(offset+j)."""
    return offset, [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs]  # type: ignore[arg-type]


def normalized_series(tail: Sequence[object]) -> LaurentSeries:
    """Build a normalized series q^-1 + tail[0] + tail[1] q + ... ."""
    return make_series(-1, [1, *tail])


def top_degree(x: LaurentSeries) -> int:
    """Largest degree whose coefficient is exactly known."""
    return x[0] + len(x[1]) - 1


def coefficient(x: LaurentSeries, degree: int) -> Fraction:
    """Coefficient of q^degree; zero below the window, error above it."""
    offset, coeffs = x
    if degree < offset:
        return Fraction(0)
    if degree > top_degree(x):
        raise IndexError(f"degree {degree} lies beyond the truncation window")
    return coeffs[degree - offset]


def multiply(x: LaurentSeries, y: LaurentSeries) -> LaurentSeries:
    """Discrete convolution, keeping only the degrees that remain exactly determined.

    Cost: O(N1 * N2) ring operations for windows of lengths N1, N2 (O(N log N) with FFT
    over a field admitting fast transforms).
    """
    dx, cx = x
    dy, cy = y
    raw: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (len(cx) + len(cy) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(cx):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cy):
            raw[i + j] += a * b
    offset = dx + dy
    reliable_top = min(top_degree(x) + dy, top_degree(y) + dx)
    return offset, raw[: max(reliable_top - offset + 1, 0)]


def product(factors: Sequence[LaurentSeries]) -> LaurentSeries:
    """Iterated convolution of a list of series.  Cost O(m N^2) for m factors."""
    if not factors:
        return make_series(0, [1])
    acc = factors[0]
    for f in factors[1:]:
        acc = multiply(acc, f)
    return acc


def pole_order(x: LaurentSeries) -> Optional[int]:
    """Return ord(x): the smallest degree with a nonzero coefficient (None if unknown)."""
    offset, coeffs = x
    for j, c in enumerate(coeffs):
        if c != 0:
            return offset + j
    return None


def shift(x: LaurentSeries, k: int) -> LaurentSeries:
    """Multiply by q^k; this moves the order by exactly k."""
    return x[0] + k, x[1]


def is_normalized(x: LaurentSeries) -> bool:
    """True iff ord(x) = -1 with leading coefficient 1."""
    o = pole_order(x)
    return o == -1 and coefficient(x, -1) == 1


def demo() -> None:

def elementary_symmetric_2(values: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Fraction:
    """e2(x) = sum_{i<j} x_i x_j, computed division-free as ((sum x)^2 - sum x^2)/2.

    Cost: O(m) additions and multiplications, O(1) extra space.
    """
    total = Fraction(0)
    squares = Fraction(0)
    for v in values:
        total += v
        squares += v * v
    return (total * total - squares) / 2


def predict_coefficients(
    linear: Sequence[object],
    quadratic: Sequence[object],
    cubic: Sequence[object],

    """Coefficients of a product of m normalized series with vanishing constant terms.

    Inputs are the coefficient vectors a_i(1), a_i(2), a_i(3) of the m factors.
    Returns a dictionary mapping degree -> coefficient for degrees -m, 1-m, 2-m, 3-m, 4-m:

        degree -m   : 1
        degree 1-m  : 0
        degree 2-m  : sum_i a_i(1)
        degree 3-m  : sum_i a_i(2)
        degree 4-m  : sum_i a_i(3) + e2(a_1(1), ..., a_m(1))

    a1: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(x) for x in linear]      # type: ignore[arg-type]
    a2: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(x) for x in quadratic]   # type: ignore[arg-type]
    a3: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(x) for x in cubic]       # type: ignore[arg-type]
    if not (len(a1) == len(a2) == len(a3)):
        raise ValueError("the three coefficient vectors must have equal length m")
    m = len(a1)
    return {
        -m: Fraction(1),
        1 - m: Fraction(0),
        2 - m: sum(a1, Fraction(0)),
        3 - m: sum(a2, Fraction(0)),
        4 - m: sum(a3, Fraction(0)) + elementary_symmetric_2(a1),

def composition_count(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """binomial(n + m - 1, m - 1): the number of terms the naive convolution would need."""
    top, k = n + m - 1, m - 1
    k = min(k, top - k)
    num, den = 1, 1
    for i in range(k):
        num *= top - i
        den *= i + 1
    return num // den

LaurentSeries = Tuple[int, List[Fraction]]


def _mk(offset: int, coeffs: Sequence[object]) -> LaurentSeries:
    return offset, [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs]  # type: ignore[arg-type]


def _top(x: LaurentSeries) -> int:
    return x[0] + len(x[1]) - 1


def _mul(x: LaurentSeries, y: LaurentSeries) -> LaurentSeries:
    dx, cx = x
    dy, cy = y
    raw: List[Fraction] = [Fraction(0)] * (len(cx) + len(cy) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(cx):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cy):
            raw[i + j] += a * b
    offset = dx + dy
    keep = min(_top(x) + dy, _top(y) + dx) - offset + 1
    return offset, raw[: max(keep, 0)]

    lo = min(x[0], y[0])
    hi = min(_top(x), _top(y))

        return s[1][d - s[0]] if s[0] <= d <= _top(s) else Fraction(0)

    return lo, [at(x, d) + at(y, d) for d in range(lo, hi + 1)]

    offset, coeffs = x

    return None

    return _mul(x, unit)

    return mask(shift(blind(x, unit), k), noise)

function top(x){ return x.d + x.c.length - 1; }

### A guided tour of the pole-order obstruction, from one integer to the Monster's 194

---

## 0. The one-sentence version

Multiply $m$ series that each begin with exactly $q^{-1}$, and the result begins with exactly $q^{-m}$ — always, with leading coefficient exactly $1$. That integer $m$ is welded on: no scrambling, no noise, no exponentiation can move it, and exactly one operation removes it. For the $194$ conjugacy classes of the Monster group, that integer is $\mathbf{194}$.

By the end of this page you will know why the integer is unremovable, what the *next* coefficients look like, and why they stay purely additive for exactly three degrees before the factors finally notice each other.

---

## 1. The playground: formal Laurent series

A **formal Laurent series** in a variable $q$ is an expression
$$f \;=\; \sum_{n \ge n_0} a_n q^n ,$$
where $n_0$ may be negative. We never worry about convergence — these are bookkeeping devices. They can be added, multiplied and (if nonzero) divided; they form a field written $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$.

The **order** $\operatorname{ord}(f)$ is the smallest exponent that actually appears. Order $-3$ means a pole of order $3$; order $+5$ means a zero of order $5$; order $0$ means finite and nonzero at the origin.

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal: why order behaves like a logarithm</strong></summary>

For nonzero $f, g$ with $N = \operatorname{ord}(f)$ and $M = \operatorname{ord}(g)$, look at the coefficient of $q^{N+M}$ in the product. It is $\sum_{j+k=N+M} f_j g_k$, and every term with $j < N$ or $k < M$ vanishes — so the only surviving term is $f_N g_M \neq 0$. Every lower coefficient vanishes for the same reason. Hence
$$\operatorname{ord}(fg) = \operatorname{ord}(f) + \operatorname{ord}(g), \qquad \mathrm{lc}(fg) = \mathrm{lc}(f)\,\mathrm{lc}(g),$$
and $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$ has no zero divisors. For sums, $\operatorname{ord}(f+g) \ge \min\{\operatorname{ord} f, \operatorname{ord} g\}$, with **equality** whenever the two orders differ — the more singular one is unopposed.

This is the whole engine. Every rigidity statement below is a corollary of these three lines. Order is a [discrete valuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valuation_(algebra)) with value group $\mathbb{Z}$.
</details>

A series is **normalized** if it looks like
$$f = q^{-1} + a(0) + a(1)q + a(2)q^2 + \cdots$$
— order exactly $-1$, leading coefficient exactly $1$. This is the shape of a [McKay–Thompson series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monstrous_moonshine) of Monstrous Moonshine. The most famous one is
$$T_{1A} = J = q^{-1} + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 + 864299970\,q^3 + \cdots,$$
and moonshine convention additionally sets the constant term to zero: $T_g = q^{-1} + O(q)$. Remember that convention — it turns out to do real mathematical work.

---

## 2. The obstruction, and playing with it

> **Pole-Order Theorem.** If $f_1,\dots,f_m$ are normalized, then $\prod_i f_i$ has order exactly $-m$ and leading coefficient $1$. Hence $q^m \prod_i f_i$ has order $0$, and $q^{m-1}\prod_i f_i$ is *again normalized*.

In particular the product of all $194$ McKay–Thompson series has a pole of order exactly $194$.

The theorem alone is easy. The interesting claim is that the integer is **unremovable**. Rather than take that on faith, attack it yourself: build a product, then try every disguise the algebra allows — multiply by an invertible power series, add noise, raise it to a power, shift it. Watch what the order does.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Things worth trying in the laboratory above:

- Load the moonshine presets and check that the pole order equals the number of factors, every time.
- Turn blinding **on** with a wild unit series. The order does not move by even one. (This is not luck: an invertible power series has order $0$, and orders add.)
- Turn masking **on**. Additive noise of higher order cannot reach past the leading term.
- Push the power slider. The order scales exactly as $-mn$ — you can never reach $0$.
- Finally press *unmask*: exactly one shift $k^\ast = -\operatorname{ord}$ works, and it works exactly.

---

## 3. Why the leak cannot be plugged

The experiments above are all shadows of one structural theorem.

> **Splitting Theorem.** The map $(u,k) \mapsto u\,q^{k}$ is a group isomorphism
> $$\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times \times \mathbb{Z} \;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\; \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times .$$
> Every nonzero Laurent series is *uniquely* an invertible power series times a power of $q$, and that exponent is its order.

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the proof</strong></summary>

It is a homomorphism because $q^kq^l = q^{k+l}$. **Injective:** if $uq^k = 1$, take orders; since $\operatorname{ord}(u)=0$ we get $k=0$, hence $u=1$. **Surjective:** given $x \neq 0$ with $N=\operatorname{ord}(x)$, the shifted series $q^{-N}x$ has order $0$, so it is a unit power series, and $x = (q^{-N}x)\,q^{N}$. $\blacksquare$

Consequence: the sequence $1 \to \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times \to \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^\times \to \mathbb{Z} \to 0$ splits, and the splitting is $k \mapsto q^k$.
</details>

Four consequences, each matching one experiment:

| you tried | theorem | statement |
|---|---|---|
| blinding | **Completeness** | $x$ and $y$ differ by an invertible power series **iff** $\operatorname{ord} x = \operatorname{ord} y$ |
| a cleverer invariant | **Rigidity** | every homomorphism to $\mathbb{Z}$ killing $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$ equals $\varphi(q)\cdot\operatorname{ord}$ |
| powers | **No roots** | $x^n$ a unit power series $\Rightarrow$ $x$ already was |
| noise | **Additive robustness** | adding anything of order $> -m$ leaves the order at $-m$ |

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal: the one-time-pad reading</strong></summary>

Call $\lambda(x) := \operatorname{ord}(x)$ the *pole leak*. Then:

* $\lambda(xu) = \lambda(x)$ for every unit power series $u$ — and conversely, the stabilizer of the leak is *exactly* $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^\times$;
* $\lambda(x\,q^k) = \lambda(x) + k$, and for any target $t$ there is a **unique** $k$ achieving it, namely $k = t - \lambda(x)$.

So the ambient group is $K \times \mathbb{Z}$, with $K$ acting as a blinding group that provably cannot touch the leak, and $\mathbb{Z}$ acting as a perfectly randomizing shift. This is the structure one wants of a [one-time pad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-time_pad) and precisely the structure one does *not* want of a side channel: no multiplicative randomization can conceal a valuation.
</details>

## 4. Beneath the leading term: three additive degrees

The order is the leading-order news. What about the next few coefficients?

There is an exact answer at every degree. Writing $a_i(-1) = 1$ for the leading $q^{-1}$ of each factor,
$$\big[q^{\,n-m}\big]\prod_{i=1}^m f_i \;=\; \sum_{\nu_1+\cdots+\nu_m=n}\ \prod_{i=1}^m a_i(\nu_i-1).$$
Exact — and useless in practice: at $m=194$ and $n=4$ that sum has $60{,}862{,}165$ terms. Its value is in how it *collapses*.

Under the moonshine normalization $a_i(0)=0$, each corrected factor is
$$q f_i = 1 + a_i(1)q^2 + a_i(2)q^3 + \cdots$$
— note the **missing $q^1$ term**. A cross term needs two factors each contributing at least $q^2$, so the earliest cross term lives in degree $4$. That single observation produces the whole hierarchy:

| degree | coefficient |
|---|---|
| $-m$ | $1$ |
| $1-m$ | $0$ |
| $2-m$ | $\sum_i a_i(1)$ |
| $3-m$ | $\sum_i a_i(2)$ |
| $4-m$ | $\sum_i a_i(3) + e_2\big(a_1(1),\dots,a_m(1)\big)$ |

where $e_2(x) = \sum_{i<j}x_ix_j = \tfrac12\big[(\sum_i x_i)^2 - \sum_i x_i^2\big]$ is the second elementary symmetric function, written division-free.

The widget below lets you *see* the mechanism as a partition count. Toggle the normalization and watch the smallest allowed part jump from $1$ to $2$, dragging the first cross term from degree $2-m$ all the way to $4-m$.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal the proof of the fourth-order identity</strong></summary>

Work with power series $g_i$ having $(g_i)_0 = 1$ and $(g_i)_1 = 0$ (these are the corrected factors $qf_i$). Induct on the number of factors. For two power series,
$$[q^4](AB) = A_0B_4 + A_1B_3 + A_2B_2 + A_3B_1 + A_4B_0 .$$
Let $A$ be the partial product of the first $k-1$ factors and $B = g_k$. By induction $A_0 = 1$, $A_1 = 0$, $A_2 = \sum_{i<k}(g_i)_2$ and $A_3 = \sum_{i<k}(g_i)_3$; and $B_0=1$, $B_1=0$. The expansion collapses to
$$[q^4](AB) = A_4 + B_4 + A_2B_2 ,$$
and the surviving cross term is
$$A_2B_2 = \Big(\sum_{i<k}(g_i)_2\Big)(g_k)_2 ,$$
which is exactly the batch of new pairwise products needed for the recursion
$$e_2(x_1,\dots,x_k) = e_2(x_1,\dots,x_{k-1}) + x_k\sum_{i<k}x_i . \qquad \blacksquare$$

The same induction with $[q^3](AB) = A_0B_3 + A_1B_2 + A_2B_1 + A_3B_0$ kills *both* middle terms and gives pure additivity at degree $3$.
</details>

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal: the generating-function explanation in one line</strong></summary>

Write $\log(q f_i) = \sum_{k\ge2}\ell_i(k)q^k$ — no linear term, because the corrected factor is $1 + O(q^2)$. Then
$$q^m\prod_i f_i = \exp\Big(\sum_{k\ge2}L_kq^k\Big), \qquad L_k = \sum_i \ell_i(k) .$$
So every coefficient is a universal polynomial in the *power sums* $L_2, L_3, \dots$, with coefficients that do not depend on $m$ at all. Degrees $2$ and $3$ can only use $L_2$ and $L_3$ linearly, because neither $2$ nor $3$ splits into two or more parts of size $\ge 2$. Degree $4$ admits $4 = 2+2$ — and that partition is the cross term.
</details>

## 5. Does it actually work? Real moonshine numbers

Take three genuine McKay–Thompson series,
$$T_{1A} = q^{-1} + 196884q + 21493760q^2 + 864299970q^3 + \cdots,$$
$$T_{2A} = q^{-1} + 4372q + 96256q^2 + 1240002q^3 + \cdots,$$
$$T_{3A} = q^{-1} + 783q + 8672q^2 + 65367q^3 + \cdots,$$
and multiply them. The hierarchy predicts, with no convolution at all:

- degree $-3$: $1$
- degree $-2$: $0$
- degree $-1$: $196884+4372+783 = 202039$
- degree $0$: $21493760+96256+8672 = 21598688$
- degree $1$: $865605339 + e_2(196884,4372,783) = 865605339 + 1018360296 = \mathbf{1883965635}$

Direct multiplication reproduces all five. Note the jump from $2\times10^{7}$ to $1.9\times10^{9}$: at the very first degree where interaction is permitted, the interaction already contributes *more than* the individual factors.

## 7. Positivity, and why moonshine cares

McKay–Thompson coefficients for the identity class are dimensions of graded pieces of an infinite-dimensional representation of the Monster — honest non-negative integers. That positivity propagates through the product, and it does so for a purely combinatorial reason.

> **Positivity.** If every factor has non-negative real coefficients, so does the product, in every degree.
>
> **Domination.** Moreover, for each factor $j$ and each $n \ge 1$,
> $$a_j(n-1) \ \le\ \big[q^{\,n-m}\big]\prod_i f_i .$$

<details>
<summary><strong>Click to reveal why domination is free</strong></summary>

In the exact convolution formula, look at the single composition that gives everything to factor $j$: $\nu_j = n$ and $\nu_i = 0$ otherwise. Its contribution is
$$a_j(n-1)\prod_{i\ne j}a_i(-1) = a_j(n-1) ,$$
since $a_i(-1)=1$. Every other contribution is a product of non-negative reals, hence non-negative. So the total is at least that one term. $\blacksquare$

An analytic-looking growth estimate, obtained with no analysis at all — just the right bookkeeping.
</details>

---

## 8. What to take away, and what is still open

The order of a Laurent series is the simplest nontrivial thing you can measure about it, and precisely because it is so simple it is maximally rigid: **complete** (it classifies series up to blinding exactly), **unique** (up to scaling, no other integer multiplicative invariant ignores blinding), **indestructible** (immune to powers and additive masking) and **repairable in exactly one way**. Nothing in that list uses $\mathbb{C}$, modularity or the Monster — it holds for any discrete valuation with value group $\mathbb{Z}$, the [$p$-adic valuation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_valuation) included. The Monster contributes only the numeral $194$, and the positivity.

Two open questions stand out.

1. **The all-order identity.** Is the degree-$(n-m)$ coefficient exactly the complete homogeneous symmetric expression in which each partition of $n$ into parts $\ge 2$ contributes once, with multinomial multiplicities? The exponential formula above makes this very plausible; the work is to organize the collapse by partitions.
2. **Rigidity without homomorphisms.** If a function $\Phi$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ is merely invariant under blinding and additive on $q^{\mathbb{Z}}$ — never assumed multiplicative anywhere else — must it be an integer multiple of the order? Invariance forces $\Phi$ to factor through the coset space, which is $\mathbb{Z}$ *as a set*; the question is whether additivity on the monomials upgrades that to additivity everywhere.

Go back to the laboratory in §2 and try to break the first claim. You will not manage it — and now you know exactly why.
